Give activated charcoal instead of NAC
Give NAC only if INR is normal
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.explanation: For staggered or unknown-time overdose, give NAC empirically; NAC is effective even late (after liver injury established) and should not be withheld.

conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.question: When is activated charcoal useful in paracetamol overdose?
options: It is never used in paracetamol overdose
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.explanation: Activated charcoal is useful if given within 1 hour of ingestion.

conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.question: What is the cause-specific treatment for autoimmune hepatitis presenting as ALF?
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.explanation: Cause-specific treatment in ALF: NAC for paracetamol, antivirals for HBV, and steroids for autoimmune hepatitis.

conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.question: At what grade of encephalopathy should the airway be secured (early intubation) in ALF?
options: Only at coma (grade IV) once apnoeic
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.explanation: Intubate early in grade III–IV encephalopathy because of the aspiration risk.

conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.question: How is raised intracranial pressure from cerebral oedema managed in the ALF ITU bundle?
options: Head-down positioning with a large bolus of IV fluids
Lactulose enemas alone, with no other ITU measures
Immediate decompressive craniectomy in every patient
Head elevated 30 degrees; mannitol or hypertonic saline
High-dose intravenous steroids and fluid restriction
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.answer: Head elevated 30 degrees; mannitol or hypertonic saline
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.explanation: Cerebral oedema is managed with the head elevated 30 degrees and mannitol or hypertonic saline for raised ICP.

conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.question: Is N-acetylcysteine used in non-paracetamol ALF?
options: Yes — it is also used in non-paracetamol ALF
No — it only works in paracetamol overdose
Only if the INR is normal
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.answer: Yes — it is also used in non-paracetamol ALF
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.explanation: NAC is also used in non-paracetamol ALF; the transplant-free survival benefit was seen in patients with early-grade encephalopathy.

conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.question: What is the single King's College Criterion sufficient to list a paracetamol-induced ALF patient for transplant?
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.explanation: For paracetamol ALF, arterial pH <7.3 (after adequate resuscitation) is a single sufficient criterion; alternatively all three of INR >6.5, creatinine >300, and grade III/IV encephalopathy.

conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.question: A patient with paracetamol ALF does not meet the pH criterion. Which combination would still satisfy the King's College Criteria?
options: A bilirubin above 300 µmol/L alone, whatever the INR and the creatinine
Age over 40 plus an unfavourable aetiology, whatever the INR or creatinine
An INR above 3.5 alone, with a normal creatinine and no encephalopathy
A jaundice-to-encephalopathy interval of more than 7 days on its own
All three of INR >6.5, creatinine >300 µmol/L, and grade III/IV encephalopathy
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.answer: All three of INR >6.5, creatinine >300 µmol/L, and grade III/IV encephalopathy
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.explanation: For paracetamol ALF, besides pH <7.3, all three of INR >6.5 (PT >100s), creatinine >300 µmol/L, and grade III/IV encephalopathy fulfil the criteria.

conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.question: For non-paracetamol ALF, which single value alone satisfies the King's College Criteria for transplantation?
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.explanation: For non-paracetamol ALF, INR >6.5 (PT >100s) alone satisfies the criteria, or any 3 of 5 factors (age <10/>40, bilirubin >300, interval >7 days, INR >3.5, unfavourable aetiology).

conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.question: Which is one of the 5 factors in the non-paracetamol King's College Criteria (3 of which are needed)?
options: An arterial pH below 7.3 after adequate resuscitation
An arterial lactate above 3.5 mmol/L after fluid resuscitation
Grade III or IV hepatic encephalopathy on admission
A serum creatinine above 300 µmol/L on admission
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.explanation: The 5 non-paracetamol factors are: age <10 or >40, bilirubin >300 µmol/L, jaundice-to-encephalopathy interval >7 days, INR >3.5, and unfavourable aetiology (drug reaction, seronegative).

conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.question: What is the only definitive treatment for non-recovering acute liver failure?
conditions__LIVER__Acute Hepatitis / Acu.explanation: Liver transplantation is the only definitive treatment for non-recovering ALF, with the King's College Criteria guiding when to list.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the decisive clinical fork that determines prognosis in liver cirrhosis?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: The decisive fork is compensated vs decompensated cirrhosis; decompensation marks the transition that carries a far worse prognosis.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Which triad of events defines decompensated cirrhosis?
options: Oliguria, rising creatinine, low urine sodium
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Decompensation is marked by encephalopathy, ascites (commonest event) and variceal haemorrhage; any one marks the transition, and 5-year survival falls from ~80% to ~20%.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the commonest decompensating event in cirrhosis?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Ascites is the commonest decompensating event in cirrhosis.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the most common cause of cirrhosis worldwide?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Hepatitis B & C are the most common cause worldwide; alcohol is the most common in the UK, and NAFLD is the fastest growing cause.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: A patient with cirrhosis has reduced caeruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings. Which cause does this indicate?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Reduced caeruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings indicate Wilson's disease.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Which autoantibody is associated with primary biliary cholangitis?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Primary biliary cholangitis is associated with anti-mitochondrial antibody (AMA). ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody point to autoimmune hepatitis, anti-LKM to type 2 autoimmune hepatitis, and p-ANCA to primary sclerosing cholangitis.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Several stigmata of chronic liver disease arise from raised oestrogen due to failed hepatic metabolism. Which sign is in this group?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Raised oestrogen causes spider naevi (>5 = significant), palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy and loss of body hair.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Which signs in cirrhosis specifically reflect portal hypertension?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Portal hypertension produces caput medusae (dilated periumbilical veins), ascites, splenomegaly and haemorrhoids.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Which blood markers are the best indicators of hepatic synthetic function in cirrhosis?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: PT + albumin are the best markers of synthetic function (raised PT + low albumin = failing liver); LFTs may be normal even in advanced cirrhosis.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the recommended hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance strategy for a patient with cirrhosis?
options: Annual contrast CT of the abdomen
6-monthly liver ultrasound, with or without serum AFP
6-monthly MRI of the liver for every patient
No surveillance unless the AFP is raised
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: 6-monthly liver ultrasound, with or without serum AFP
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Surveillance is 6-monthly liver ultrasound, with or without serum AFP (NICE). AFP is neither sensitive nor specific, so it neither confirms nor excludes HCC; a suspicious lesion is characterised on four-phase CT or MRI.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What does the 'D' represent in the Child-Pugh (ABCDE) score?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Child-Pugh ABCDE = Albumin, Bilirubin, Clotting (PT), Dilation (ascites), Encephalopathy.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: A cirrhotic patient has a Child-Pugh score of 12. Which class and prognosis does this represent?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Child-Pugh Class C (10–15 points) indicates decompensated cirrhosis with poor prognosis (Class A 5–6 well-compensated; Class B 7–9 significant impairment).

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Which components make up the UKELD score, used for UK liver transplant listing?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: UKELD uses sodium, bilirubin, creatinine and INR, and is the score used for liver transplant listing in the UK. MELD (bilirubin, creatinine, INR) is the equivalent score used internationally.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Above what hepatic venous pressure gradient is portal hypertension clinically significant — the threshold at which varices form and β-blocker prophylaxis is considered?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Clinically significant portal hypertension is an HVPG above 10 mmHg — the point at which varices form and prophylaxis is considered. Normal HVPG is 1–5 mmHg, and above 12 mmHg is the threshold at which varices bleed.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Budd-Chiari syndrome is which type of cause of portal hypertension?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis) is a post-hepatic cause of portal hypertension.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the HCC surveillance schedule in cirrhosis?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: HCC surveillance is AFP + USS every 6 months; OGD every 3 years screens for varices in compensated cirrhosis.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: A cirrhotic patient presents with an acute variceal bleed. What is the target haemoglobin for transfusion, and why is over-transfusion avoided?
options: 70–80 g/L, because over-transfusion raises portal pressure
100–110 g/L, because higher Hb improves clotting
Above 120 g/L, to maximise oxygen delivery
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: 70–80 g/L, because over-transfusion raises portal pressure
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Target Hb is 70–80 g/L; over-transfusion is avoided because it raises portal pressure and can worsen bleeding.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: A patient with a variceal bleed cannot be given terlipressin. Which vasoactive agent is used off-licence in the UK instead?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Terlipressin requires particular care — rather than being absolutely contraindicated — in ischaemic heart disease. Where it is judged unsuitable, octreotide or somatostatin is used off-licence in the UK on senior advice.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Which antibiotic is given in acute variceal haemorrhage, and what is the key benefit?
options: IV ceftriaxone — reduces SBP and mortality
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: IV ceftriaxone — reduces SBP and mortality
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Prophylactic IV broad-spectrum antibiotics are offered at presentation to anyone with suspected or confirmed variceal bleeding; they reduce infection and mortality. Ceftriaxone is commonly used, according to local microbiology policy.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the definitive endoscopic treatment of choice for oesophageal variceal haemorrhage?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Urgent OGD + band ligation is the treatment of choice; sclerotherapy is used only if ligation is not possible.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Band ligation fails to control a variceal bleed. A Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is placed as a bridge. What is its maximum duration and a key risk?
options: Maximum 1 hour; risk of portal vein thrombosis
Maximum 24 hours; risks include oesophageal rupture
Maximum 7 days; risk of hepatorenal syndrome
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: Maximum 24 hours; risks include oesophageal rupture
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Balloon tamponade is a bridge to definitive treatment, ideally in critical care, and should not be left in place beyond 24 hours; risks include aspiration pneumonia, oesophageal ulceration and rupture.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the agent of choice for secondary prevention of variceal haemorrhage?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Propranolol (a non-selective β-blocker) reduces cardiac output and causes splanchnic vasoconstriction, lowering portal pressure; it is started after the acute bleed settles, with repeat band ligation every 2 weeks.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: A diagnostic ascitic tap shows a SAAG of >11 g/L. What does this indicate?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: SAAG >11 g/L indicates a transudate from portal hypertension (cirrhosis, cardiac, Budd-Chiari); SAAG <11 g/L indicates an exudate (malignancy, peritoneal TB, pancreatitis).

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: In the stepwise management of ascites, which diuretic is first-line and at what starting dose?
options: Furosemide 40 mg OD, titrated up to 160 mg
Spironolactone 100 mg OD, titrated up to 400 mg
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: Spironolactone 100 mg OD, titrated up to 400 mg
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Spironolactone (an aldosterone antagonist) is first-line at 100 mg OD, titrated up to 400 mg, with furosemide added if needed (ratio 100:40), after sodium restriction.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: After a large-volume paracentesis for tense ascites, what should be given and why?
options: A bolus of normal saline, to prevent hypernatraemia after the drain
20% albumin (6–8 g/L drained) to prevent circulatory dysfunction
Spironolactone at a higher dose, to prevent re-accumulation of the ascites
Prophylactic ceftriaxone, to prevent spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Nothing further is required after an uncomplicated large-volume drain
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: 20% albumin (6–8 g/L drained) to prevent circulatory dysfunction
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: 20% albumin (6–8 g per litre drained) is given to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: A cirrhotic patient with ascites develops fever, abdominal pain and worsening encephalopathy. An ascitic tap shows neutrophils >250 cells/mm³. What is the management principle?
options: Await culture results from the ascitic fluid before starting any treatment
Start oral ciprofloxacin prophylaxis only, and review in the morning
Perform urgent TIPS to decompress the portal system
Treat SBP immediately with IV broad-spectrum antibiotics — do not wait for culture
Give terlipressin alone and repeat the ascitic tap in 48 hours
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: Treat SBP immediately with IV broad-spectrum antibiotics — do not wait for culture
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Ascitic neutrophils >250 cells/mm³ diagnose SBP and should be treated immediately with empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics per local policy — commonly piperacillin-tazobactam, or a third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime — for 5 days, plus 20% albumin. Do not wait for culture.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the most common organism causing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: E. coli is the most common organism in SBP, a common and often silent complication of cirrhotic ascites that is substantially more frequent in hospitalised patients.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Why is 20% albumin given alongside antibiotics in SBP?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: 20% albumin (1.5 g/kg day 1 + 1 g/kg day 3) is given alongside antibiotics in SBP to reduce hepatorenal syndrome risk.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: After a first episode of SBP, what long-term prophylaxis is recommended, and what referral is indicated?
options: Long-term IV ceftriaxone; no referral needed
Lifelong lactulose; refer to gastroenterology only
Long-term oral ciprofloxacin; refer for liver transplant
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: Long-term oral ciprofloxacin; refer for liver transplant
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Long-term oral ciprofloxacin is given after an episode of SBP, and as primary prophylaxis if the ascitic protein is 15 g/L or less until the ascites resolves (NICE). Norfloxacin appears in older texts but is no longer available in the UK. SBP is an indication for liver transplant referral.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the principal toxin implicated in the mechanism of hepatic encephalopathy?
options: Ammonia from gut bacterial metabolism of proteins
Free fatty acids from fat necrosis
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: Ammonia from gut bacterial metabolism of proteins
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy results from toxins, principally ammonia from gut bacterial metabolism of proteins, bypassing the diseased liver and reaching the brain (astrocyte swelling + neurotransmitter disruption).

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: A cirrhotic patient is confused with a flapping tremor and sweet musty breath, and cannot draw a 5-pointed star. Which combination of signs is this?
options: Kayser-Fleischer rings, caput medusae and leukonychia
Spider naevi, palmar erythema and gynaecomastia
Cullen's sign, Grey-Turner's sign and tetany
Asterixis, fetor hepaticus and constructional apraxia
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: Asterixis, fetor hepaticus and constructional apraxia
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: These are features of hepatic encephalopathy: asterixis (flapping tremor), fetor hepaticus (sweet musty breath) and constructional apraxia (can't draw a 5-pointed star).

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: How does lactulose help in hepatic encephalopathy?
options: It lowers colonic pH, reducing ammonia production and absorption
It directly binds circulating ammonia in the bloodstream
It sterilises the entire gut, removing all bacteria
It increases protein absorption from the small bowel
It raises the colonic pH in order to neutralise toxins
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: It lowers colonic pH, reducing ammonia production and absorption
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Lactulose is an osmotic purgative that lowers colonic pH, reducing ammonia-producing bacteria and ammonia absorption, targeting 2–3 soft stools/day; rifaximin reduces ammonia-producing gut flora.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Regarding nutrition in hepatic encephalopathy, which statement is correct?
options: Protein must be completely eliminated from the diet
A high-protein diet does NOT worsen encephalopathy
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: A high-protein diet does NOT worsen encephalopathy
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Adequate nutrition is important; a high-protein diet does NOT worsen encephalopathy.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Which of the following is a recognised precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy?
options: Regular lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools a day
High urine output from fluid loading
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Precipitants include GI bleed, infection, constipation, dehydration, sedatives/opioids, electrolyte disturbance and over-diuresis. Note that over-purgation with laxatives can itself precipitate encephalopathy through dehydration and electrolyte loss, which is why lactulose is titrated to 2–3 soft stools a day rather than given to maximal effect.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: A patient with advanced cirrhosis and ascites develops AKI with bland urine microscopy, and does not improve after diuretics are stopped and 2 days of IV albumin. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Hepatorenal syndrome is AKI in cirrhosis with ascites, diagnosed by exclusion: no sustained improvement after stopping diuretics and 2 days of IV 20% albumin, no shock, no recent nephrotoxins and no structural kidney disease. A very low urine sodium is typical but is no longer a diagnostic criterion.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the mechanism of hepatorenal syndrome?
options: Direct nephrotoxic injury to the tubules from circulating bilirubin and bile salts
Glomerular immune complex deposition producing an acute nephritic picture
Mechanical obstruction of the renal tract by the weight of the ascites itself
Splanchnic vasodilation → ↓effective circulating volume → RAAS → renal vasoconstriction
Acute tubular necrosis driven by sepsis and circulating bacterial endotoxin
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: Splanchnic vasodilation → ↓effective circulating volume → RAAS → renal vasoconstriction
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Hepatorenal syndrome arises from splanchnic vasodilation reducing effective circulating volume, activating RAAS, causing renal vasoconstriction and reduced GFR, with no intrinsic renal pathology.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the definitive treatment offering the best prognosis in hepatorenal syndrome?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Hepatorenal syndrome has a poor prognosis without liver transplantation (managed meanwhile with terlipressin, 20% albumin, stopping nephrotoxins, and TIPS in selected patients); refer urgently.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: A patient has tender hepatomegaly and ascites but no cirrhosis, with hepatic vein thrombosis on imaging. What is the diagnosis and management?
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Budd-Chiari syndrome is post-hepatic portal hypertension from hepatic vein thrombosis: tender hepatomegaly + ascites + no cirrhosis; managed with anticoagulation + TIPS.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the cirrhosis care bundle?
options: A long-term outpatient monitoring schedule for people with compensated cirrhosis
A surgical protocol governing the conduct of liver transplantation
A scoring system that predicts the risk of variceal rebleeding
A palliative care pathway for patients with end-stage liver disease
A checklist applied in the first 24 hours of an admission with decompensated cirrhosis
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: A checklist applied in the first 24 hours of an admission with decompensated cirrhosis
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: The decompensated cirrhosis care bundle (BSG) is applied within the first 24 hours of an admission with decompensated cirrhosis to standardise early care and reduce preventable mortality.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Within what timeframe should a diagnostic ascitic tap be performed in the care bundle, and what is the key caveat?
options: Only once the clotting has been corrected with FFP
Within 24 h to exclude SBP; deranged clotting is no bar
Within 1 week, if the patient remains febrile
Only if the ascites is tense and uncomfortable
Never — paracentesis is contraindicated in cirrhosis
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: Within 24 h to exclude SBP; deranged clotting is no bar
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: A diagnostic ascitic tap is done within 24 hours to exclude SBP (neutrophils >250); deranged clotting is not a contraindication and must not delay it.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: A patient admitted with decompensated cirrhosis has a suspected variceal bleed. Which combination does the care bundle specify?
options: A proton-pump inhibitor infusion on its own
Immediate TIPS for every patient who bleeds
Transfusion to a target Hb above 100 g/L
Starting a beta-blocker during the acute bleed
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: The variceal-bleed arm is terlipressin + prophylactic IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone) + OGD with band ligation within 24 hours; beta-blockers are for secondary prevention, not the acute bleed.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: What is the transfusion target for a variceal bleed in the care bundle, and why?
options: Restrictive Hb 70–80 g/L, because over-transfusion raises portal pressure
A target Hb above 100 g/L, to improve clotting and haemostasis
A target Hb above 120 g/L, to maximise oxygen delivery to the liver
No transfusion is ever given in a variceal bleed
A target Hb of 50–60 g/L, to keep the portal pressure as low as possible
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: Restrictive Hb 70–80 g/L, because over-transfusion raises portal pressure
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: A restrictive target of Hb 70–80 g/L is used because over-transfusion raises portal pressure and can worsen variceal bleeding.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: In an alcohol-dependent patient admitted with decompensated cirrhosis, why is thiamine given before glucose-containing fluids?
options: Glucose inactivates the antibiotics given for sepsis
Thiamine directly lowers the circulating ammonia level
A glucose load without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's
Glucose worsens the ascites by retaining sodium
Thiamine must be given on an empty stomach to absorb
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: A glucose load without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: A carbohydrate load without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy, so thiamine is given before or alongside glucose-containing fluids. Hypoglycaemia is the exception — treat it immediately and give thiamine alongside.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: Which is an indication for human albumin within the cirrhosis care bundle?
options: All patients with compensated cirrhosis, given as a routine infusion
Routine nutritional supplementation in malnourished cirrhotic patients
To reverse hepatic encephalopathy directly by binding ammonia
As the first-line resuscitation fluid in acute variceal bleeding
SBP, large-volume paracentesis, or hepatorenal syndrome
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: SBP, large-volume paracentesis, or hepatorenal syndrome
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Human albumin is indicated for SBP, large-volume paracentesis (post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction) and hepatorenal syndrome.

conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.question: How does the cirrhosis care bundle manage hepatic encephalopathy on admission?
options: High-dose sedation to settle the agitation
Identify and treat the precipitant; lactulose ± rifaximin
Protein restriction as the first-line measure
Immediate haemodialysis to clear the ammonia
Withhold all laxatives until the confusion clears
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.answer: Identify and treat the precipitant; lactulose ± rifaximin
conditions__LIVER__Liver Cirrhosis.explanation: Encephalopathy is managed by finding and treating the precipitant (infection, GI bleed, constipation, dehydration, sedatives, electrolytes) and giving lactulose ± rifaximin; sedatives are avoided.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: What is the defining principle governing damage in alcoholic liver disease?
options: Damage is always fully reversible with abstinence
Damage is irreversible from the very first drink
Damage only occurs after cirrhosis develops
Damage is reversible early but irreversible late
Damage is unrelated to the quantity of alcohol
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Damage is reversible early but irreversible late
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Alcoholic liver disease results from chronic excessive alcohol consumption; the defining principle is that damage is reversible early and irreversible late.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: Which sequence correctly represents the stepwise progression of alcoholic liver disease?
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Hepatic steatosis → alcoholic hepatitis → cirrhosis
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: The progression is hepatic steatosis (reversible) → alcoholic hepatitis (partly reversible) → cirrhosis (irreversible fibrosis + nodular regeneration).

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: What is the UK Chief Medical Officers' recommended weekly alcohol limit?
options: ≤14 units/week for both men and women
No specific limit, only avoid binges
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: ≤14 units/week for both men and women
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: UK Chief Medical Officers' guidance is ≤14 units/week for both men and women, spread evenly over 3 or more days. It sets no daily unit limit — the weekly guideline deliberately replaced the old daily benchmarks. Single-occasion advice is to limit the total drunk, drink slowly, with food, and alternate with water.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: Using the UK statistical definition, a binge for women is:
options: More than 8 units in a session
More than 14 units in a session
More than 3 units in a session
More than 10 units in a session
More than 6 units in a session
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: More than 6 units in a session
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: A binge is more than 6 units in a single session for women, and more than 8 units for men.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: Using the unit formula, how many units are in 250 mL of 13% wine?
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: 3.3 units
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Units = (ABV% × volume in mL) ÷ 1000, so 13 × 250 ÷ 1000 = 3.25 ≈ 3.3 units (consistent with the worked example).

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: A patient with alcoholic hepatitis presents acutely. Which set of features is most characteristic?
options: Painless jaundice and a palpable gallbladder
Epigastric pain radiating to the back with raised amylase
Jaundice, RUQ pain, fever, tender hepatomegaly
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Jaundice, RUQ pain, fever, tender hepatomegaly
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Acute alcoholic hepatitis presents with jaundice (raised bilirubin), RUQ pain, fever, tender hepatomegaly and ascites in severe cases.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: Which finding identifies severe alcohol-related hepatitis and a high short-term mortality?
options: A Maddrey discriminant function of 32 or more
An AST:ALT ratio of 2:1 or more
An MCV above the reference range
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: A Maddrey discriminant function of 32 or more
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: A discriminant function ≥32 defines severe disease, carries a high short-term mortality, and identifies patients who may be offered corticosteroids (NICE). The other findings indicate alcohol use or steatosis but do not grade severity.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: An AST:ALT ratio of ≥2:1 most strongly suggests which diagnosis?
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Alcoholic liver disease
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: An AST:ALT ratio ≥2:1 suggests alcoholic liver disease; in viral hepatitis and NAFLD, ALT > AST.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: Which blood enzyme is characteristically elevated and a sensitive marker of alcohol use?
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: GGT
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: GGT is characteristically elevated in alcohol-related liver disease and is a sensitive marker of alcohol use — but it is not specific, also rising with cholestasis, metabolic fatty liver disease, obesity and enzyme-inducing drugs.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: Which combination of blood results indicates impaired hepatic synthetic function in alcoholic liver disease?
options: Raised bilirubin and raised AST alone
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Low albumin and raised PT/INR
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Reduced albumin and raised PT/INR reflect impaired synthetic function.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: Why are platelets often low in alcoholic liver disease?
options: Direct bone marrow toxicity from bilirubin
Splenic vein thrombosis from a tumour
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Portal hypertension causing hypersplenism
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Low platelets result from portal hypertension leading to hypersplenism.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: Why is the MCV typically raised in alcoholic liver disease?
options: Direct alcohol toxicity plus B-vitamin deficiency
Iron deficiency from poor dietary intake
Chronic occult blood loss from varices
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Direct alcohol toxicity plus B-vitamin deficiency
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Macrocytosis (raised MCV) arises from direct alcohol toxicity and B-vitamin deficiency.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: Which histological finding on liver biopsy is characteristic of alcoholic hepatitis?
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Mallory-Denk bodies
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Liver biopsy is the reference standard for histological staging; Mallory-Denk bodies are seen in alcohol-related hepatitis.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: A patient with alcoholic hepatitis has a Maddrey's discriminant function of 36. What does this indicate?
options: Severe disease — a candidate for steroids
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Severe disease — a candidate for steroids
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Maddrey's DF ≥32 = severe disease and identifies a steroid candidate (prednisolone 40 mg/day for 28 days).

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: A patient with severe alcoholic hepatitis is started on prednisolone. How is treatment response assessed and when?
options: Maddrey's DF repeated at day 28; if below 32, continue
Lille score at day 7; if >0.45, stop steroids as there is no benefit
CIWA-Ar score measured daily; if it stays high, continue
FibroScan on day 1; if it shows cirrhosis, stop treatment
AST:ALT ratio at day 14; if below 2, continue treatment
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Lille score at day 7; if >0.45, stop steroids as there is no benefit
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: The Lille score at day 7 assesses response; if there is no improvement (score >0.45), steroids are stopped as they provide no benefit.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: A patient with severe alcohol-related hepatitis (discriminant function 38) has an active upper GI bleed. What is the correct approach to corticosteroids?
options: Start prednisolone immediately, alongside endoscopy for the bleed
Give pentoxifylline instead of corticosteroids, as it is safer here
Withhold all treatment permanently — steroids are absolutely barred
Treat the bleed first — steroids may follow once bleeding is controlled
Start acamprosate in place of corticosteroids until bleeding settles
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Treat the bleed first — steroids may follow once bleeding is controlled
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Corticosteroids are offered for severe alcohol-related hepatitis with a discriminant function ≥32, but only after active infection or gastrointestinal bleeding has been effectively treated (NICE) — these are reasons to delay, not permanent bars. Pentoxifylline does not improve survival and is no longer recommended. Acamprosate is for maintaining abstinence, not acute hepatitis.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: Which statement best reflects current UK practice on referring a patient with decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis for liver transplant assessment?
options: Refer and discuss early — a fixed 6-month abstinence rule is no longer applied
Referral requires exactly 6 months of documented abstinence beforehand
Transplantation is never offered in alcohol-related liver disease
Abstinence and engagement with alcohol services are irrelevant here
Referral is only made once a Lille score has been calculated
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Refer and discuss early — a fixed 6-month abstinence rule is no longer applied
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: UK guidance advises against basing referral on the 6-month 'rule of thumb'; early discussion with the transplant centre is encouraged where the patient is abstinent and engaged with alcohol services.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: What is the neurochemical mechanism of alcohol withdrawal?
options: Chronic alcohol upregulates GABA receptors, so withdrawal causes deep sedation
Withdrawal depletes dopamine in the basal ganglia, and this causes the seizures
Chronic alcohol downregulates GABA and upregulates NMDA → unopposed excitability
Withdrawal raises cortical serotonin, and this causes the hallucinations
Withdrawal directly blocks NMDA receptors, reducing excitatory transmission
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Chronic alcohol downregulates GABA and upregulates NMDA → unopposed excitability
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Chronic alcohol reduces GABA receptors and increases NMDA receptors (compensatory); sudden withdrawal leaves unopposed CNS excitability, causing seizures and delirium tremens.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: A patient stopped drinking 36 hours ago and develops confusion, agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, sweating and fever. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Delirium tremens
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Delirium tremens occurs at 24–72 h: confusion, agitation and autonomic instability (raised HR/BP, sweating, fever). It is a medical emergency and carries significant mortality if untreated.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: Within what timeframe after the last drink do generalised tonic-clonic withdrawal seizures typically occur?
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: 24–48 hours
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Generalised tonic-clonic seizures (withdrawal fits) typically occur 24–48 hours after the last drink.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: What is the first-line drug for managing alcohol withdrawal, and what tool guides dosing?
options: Oral haloperidol, guided by Maddrey's DF
IV thiamine, guided by the Lille score
Oral chlordiazepoxide, guided by the CIWA-Ar scale
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Oral chlordiazepoxide, guided by the CIWA-Ar scale
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Benzodiazepines (oral chlordiazepoxide in a reducing regimen over 5–7 days) are first-line, with a symptom-triggered regimen such as CIWA-Ar guiding dosing. In liver impairment prefer a benzodiazepine needing little hepatic metabolism, such as lorazepam, at reduced dose — and avoid benzodiazepines altogether in severe liver impairment (NICE). Do not use phenytoin for alcohol withdrawal seizures.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: Why should haloperidol not be used alone in delirium tremens?
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: It lowers the seizure threshold
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Haloperidol should not be used alone in DTs because it lowers the seizure threshold.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: An alcohol-dependent patient arrives confused, with a normal blood glucose, and IV glucose-containing fluids are about to be started. Why should thiamine be given first?
options: Glucose inactivates thiamine within the gut lumen
Thiamine raises the blood glucose dangerously fast
A glucose load without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's
Glucose causes immediate delirium tremens in withdrawal
Thiamine must be given on an empty stomach to be absorbed
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: A glucose load without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: A carbohydrate load without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke's encephalopathy, so thiamine is given before or alongside glucose-containing fluids. Hypoglycaemia is the exception: treat it immediately and give parenteral thiamine alongside — never delay glucose.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: A patient presents with confusion, ophthalmoplegia with nystagmus, and ataxia. What is the diagnosis and immediate treatment?
options: Delirium tremens — give oral lorazepam now
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Wernicke's encephalopathy — parenteral high-dose thiamine
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: The triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia is Wernicke's encephalopathy. Treat immediately with parenteral high-dose thiamine, continued for a minimum of 5 days then oral thiamine (NICE). The full triad is present in only a minority, so treat on suspicion.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: A patient with a history of untreated Wernicke's now has anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation. What is the diagnosis and prognosis?
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Korsakoff syndrome — chronic and irreversible
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Korsakoff syndrome is the chronic, irreversible consequence of untreated/recurrent Wernicke's: anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation; residential/nursing care is often required.

conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.question: What is confabulation, as seen in Korsakoff syndrome?
options: Loss of the ability to speak
Unconscious fabrication of memories to fill gaps
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.answer: Unconscious fabrication of memories to fill gaps
conditions__LIVER__Alcoholic Liver Disea.explanation: Confabulation is the unconscious fabrication of memories to fill gaps, a feature of Korsakoff syndrome.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Which statement best describes where glycolysis occurs and its oxygen requirement?
options: In the mitochondrial matrix, requiring oxygen
In the cytoplasm, requiring oxygen only
In the mitochondrial matrix, without oxygen
In the cytoplasm, with or without oxygen
On the inner mitochondrial membrane, requiring oxygen
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: In the cytoplasm, with or without oxygen
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm of every cell and can run either aerobically or anaerobically — no mitochondria or oxygen are needed, which is why it serves as the emergency energy pathway.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: What is the net yield of glycolysis per molecule of glucose?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: 2 ATP net + 2 NADH + 2 pyruvate
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: The payoff phase produces 4 ATP, but 2 ATP were invested in the investment phase, giving a net of 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate per glucose.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: During the investment phase of glycolysis, what happens to the 2 ATP that are used?
options: They convert glucose directly to lactate
They regenerate NAD⁺ for continued glycolysis
They phosphorylate glucose, trapping it in the cell
They are harvested as electron carriers
They combine with oxaloacetate to form citrate
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: They phosphorylate glucose, trapping it in the cell
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: In the investment phase, 2 ATP are used to phosphorylate glucose, which traps it inside the cell and primes it for the subsequent splitting and processing in the payoff phase.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Which enzyme catalyses the rate-limiting, committed step of glycolysis?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1)
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: PFK-1 catalyses the rate-limiting, committed step of glycolysis — the main control point of the pathway.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: How is PFK-1 activity regulated to match cellular energy needs?
options: Activated by ATP and citrate; inhibited by AMP
Activated by AMP/ADP; inhibited by ATP and citrate
Activated by NADH; inhibited by NAD⁺
Activated by glucagon; inhibited by insulin
Activated by oxygen; inhibited by lactate
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Activated by AMP/ADP; inhibited by ATP and citrate
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: PFK-1 is activated by AMP/ADP (signalling low energy → speed glycolysis up) and inhibited by ATP and citrate (signalling high energy → slow it down), so the cell makes ATP when it needs it.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A patient in the fed state has high circulating insulin. What effect does this have on glycolysis?
options: Insulin inhibits glycolysis to preserve glucose
Insulin has no effect on glycolysis
Insulin converts pyruvate directly to lactate
Insulin stimulates glycolysis to use/store glucose
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Insulin stimulates glycolysis to use/store glucose
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Insulin stimulates glycolysis in the fed state (use/store glucose), whereas glucagon inhibits it in the fasted state (preserve glucose) — cross-referencing glucose homeostasis.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A marathon runner's leg muscles are working beyond their oxygen supply, producing a burning sensation. Which process is occurring, and what is the ATP yield?
options: Anaerobic glycolysis → pyruvate converted to lactate, 2 ATP
Anaerobic glycolysis → pyruvate converted to acetyl-CoA, 2 ATP
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Anaerobic glycolysis → pyruvate converted to lactate, 2 ATP
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: When O₂ demand exceeds supply in exercising muscle, glycolysis runs anaerobically, converting pyruvate to lactate (via lactate dehydrogenase) — this yields only 2 ATP and produces lactate ('the burn').

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Why is the conversion of pyruvate to lactate essential for anaerobic glycolysis to continue?
options: It regenerates oxygen for the cell to use
It regenerates NAD⁺, which glycolysis needs
It produces acetyl-CoA for the Krebs cycle
It removes citrate that would inhibit PFK-1
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: It regenerates NAD⁺, which glycolysis needs
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Glycolysis consumes NAD⁺ (making NADH). Aerobically, mitochondria regenerate NAD⁺; anaerobically, converting pyruvate → lactate regenerates NAD⁺, allowing glycolysis and thus ATP production to continue without oxygen.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Which cell type relies entirely on glycolysis for its energy because it lacks mitochondria?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Red blood cells
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Red blood cells have no mitochondria, so they rely entirely on glycolysis (always anaerobic) — cross-referencing red cell physiology.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A patient with septic shock has a raised serum lactate and a raised-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Which mechanism best explains the raised lactate?
options: Tissue hypoperfusion driving anaerobic glycolysis to lactate
Reduced pyruvate kinase activity in red cells
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Tissue hypoperfusion driving anaerobic glycolysis to lactate
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: A raised lactate is a marker of tissue hypoperfusion, used to grade severity in sepsis and shock — but it is not specific.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Cancer cells preferentially use glycolysis even when oxygen is present. What is this phenomenon called, and what imaging modality does it underpin?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: The Warburg effect; PET (FDG) imaging
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Cancer cells preferentially use glycolysis even with O₂ present (the Warburg effect). This tumour reliance on glycolysis is the basis of PET (FDG) imaging.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Which enzyme deficiency is the commonest glycolytic cause of hereditary non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Pyruvate kinase deficiency
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Red cells depend on glycolysis (no mitochondria). Pyruvate kinase deficiency impairs glycolytic ATP production in RBCs, leading to haemolysis.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Where does the Krebs cycle take place, and what is its two-carbon input?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Mitochondrial matrix; acetyl-CoA
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: The Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix (unlike glycolysis, which is in the cytoplasm), and its input is acetyl-CoA (2 carbons).

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: What is the output of a single turn of the Krebs cycle?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ + 1 GTP + 2 CO₂
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: One turn of the Krebs cycle yields 3 NADH + 1 FADH₂ + 1 GTP (≈ATP) + 2 CO₂.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Why does the Krebs cycle turn twice per molecule of glucose?
options: Because each glucose produces 2 GTP directly
Because oxaloacetate is used up each turn
Because two oxygen molecules are required
Because the cycle produces 2 CO₂ per glucose
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Because glycolysis produces 2 pyruvate → 2 acetyl-CoA
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Glycolysis makes 2 pyruvate per glucose → 2 acetyl-CoA → 2 turns of the cycle, so the per-cycle output is doubled.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Although the Krebs cycle has no direct oxygen-consuming step, it stops without oxygen. Why?
options: Oxygen is a direct substrate of citrate synthase
Oxygen is needed to convert pyruvate to acetyl-CoA
Lactate accumulation directly inhibits the cycle
NAD⁺ and FAD cannot be regenerated, so the cycle halts
Oxygen is required to regenerate oxaloacetate
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: NAD⁺ and FAD cannot be regenerated, so the cycle halts
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: The cycle consumes NAD⁺ and FAD (converting them to NADH/FADH₂). These must be regenerated by oxidative phosphorylation, which needs O₂. Without O₂, NADH/FADH₂ can't be reoxidised → NAD⁺/FAD run out → the cycle halts.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: What is the primary purpose of the Krebs cycle, rather than direct ATP production?
options: To harvest electrons as NADH and FADH₂
To produce large amounts of ATP directly (over 30 per turn)
To generate lactate for anaerobic tissue
To store surplus energy as fatty acids
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: To harvest electrons as NADH and FADH₂
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: The cycle's real job is not to make ATP directly (only 1 GTP) — it is to harvest high-energy electrons as NADH + FADH₂, which are then 'cashed in' for lots of ATP in oxidative phosphorylation.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: In the link reaction, pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA. Which enzyme complex catalyses this, and what else is produced?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH); producing CO₂ + NADH
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: The pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex catalyses pyruvate → acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH before the cycle.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A malnourished patient with chronic alcohol dependence presents with confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia. Which vitamin cofactor deficiency, affecting pyruvate metabolism, best explains this presentation?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Vitamin B1 (thiamine)
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: PDH (and a Krebs enzyme) require thiamine (B1) as a cofactor. Thiamine deficiency (alcoholism, malnutrition) impairs pyruvate metabolism → lactate build-up and energy failure → Wernicke's encephalopathy/beriberi. This is why alcoholics receive IV thiamine (Pabrinex).

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Why is the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) step described as a key irreversible commitment?
options: Because acetyl-CoA can be readily converted back to glucose
Acetyl-CoA is committed to oxidation and cannot return to glucose
Because it produces GTP that cannot be reused
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Acetyl-CoA is committed to oxidation and cannot return to glucose
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Once pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA, it is committed to oxidation and cannot go back to glucose — making PDH a key irreversible commitment point.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: How do the three macronutrients converge on the Krebs cycle?
options: All are converted to pyruvate before entering
Only carbohydrates can enter the cycle
Fat enters as lactate, protein as pyruvate, carbohydrate as citrate
Carbohydrate, fat and protein all converge on acetyl-CoA
All three enter exclusively as oxaloacetate
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Carbohydrate, fat and protein all converge on acetyl-CoA
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Carbohydrate enters via glucose → glycolysis → pyruvate → acetyl-CoA; fat via fatty acids → β-oxidation → acetyl-CoA; protein via amino acids → various cycle intermediates (or acetyl-CoA). This makes the cycle the common final pathway for all fuels.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: The Krebs cycle is described as both catabolic and biosynthetic. Which statement best explains its biosynthetic role?
options: Its intermediates are building blocks for other molecules
It directly synthesises ATP for storage
It produces oxygen for other pathways
It converts lactate back into pyruvate
It generates fatty acids from NADH
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Its intermediates are building blocks for other molecules
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Cycle intermediates are also building blocks — for amino acids, glucose via gluconeogenesis, and haem — so the cycle is both catabolic and a biosynthetic hub.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: How is the Krebs cycle regulated by the cell's energy state?
options: ↑ATP/NADH speeds it up; ↑ADP/NAD⁺ slows it down
It is regulated only by oxygen concentration
↑ATP/NADH slows it down; ↑ADP/NAD⁺ speeds it up
It is regulated only by insulin and glucagon
It runs at a constant rate regardless of energy state
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: ↑ATP/NADH slows it down; ↑ADP/NAD⁺ speeds it up
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: The cycle is controlled by the cell's energy state: high energy (↑ATP/NADH) slows the cycle, while low energy (↑ADP/NAD⁺) speeds it up — similar to glycolysis. Isocitrate dehydrogenase (and others), plus PDH at the entry, are key regulated enzymes.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A patient in shock has no oxygen delivery to a peripheral tissue. Which statement best explains why that tissue must rely on glycolysis + lactate for ATP?
options: Glycolysis is faster than oxidative phosphorylation even with oxygen
The Krebs cycle continues without oxygen indefinitely
Oxygen inhibits glycolysis, so its absence boosts ATP
Glycolysis to lactate becomes the only ATP source
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Glycolysis to lactate becomes the only ATP source
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Without O₂, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation stop (NAD⁺/FAD cannot be regenerated), so glycolysis → lactate becomes the only remaining ATP source in anaerobic tissue.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Where does oxidative phosphorylation take place, and what does it require?
options: In the cytoplasm, requiring NADH only
On the inner mitochondrial membrane, requiring NADH + FADH₂ + O₂
In the mitochondrial matrix, requiring acetyl-CoA
On the outer mitochondrial membrane, requiring O₂ only
In the cytoplasm, with or without oxygen
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: On the inner mitochondrial membrane, requiring NADH + FADH₂ + O₂
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Oxidative phosphorylation occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane. Its inputs are NADH + FADH₂ (from glycolysis, the link reaction and Krebs) plus O₂, and it produces the bulk of the cell's ATP + water.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Approximately how many of the ~30–32 ATP produced per glucose come from oxidative phosphorylation?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: ~26–28 ATP (the vast majority)
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: The ATP tally per glucose is glycolysis (2) + Krebs GTP (2) + oxidative phosphorylation (~26–28) = ~30–32 total, showing that oxidative phosphorylation makes the vast majority (glycolysis alone gives only 2).

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: In the electron transport chain, how is the energy from electrons initially captured before ATP is made?
options: As a proton (H⁺) gradient across the inner membrane
It is transferred directly to ADP by the complexes
It is stored as heat in brown fat
It is used to reduce oxygen to lactate
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: As a proton (H⁺) gradient across the inner membrane
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: As electrons pass down the chain (losing energy), that energy pumps protons (H⁺) out of the matrix, building an electrochemical gradient (the proton-motive force). Per the chemiosmotic theory, energy is stored as this proton gradient rather than transferred directly.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: What is the role of ATP synthase (Complex V) in chemiosmosis?
options: It pumps protons out of the matrix
It donates its electrons to oxygen
Protons flow back through it, making ATP
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Protons flow back through it, making ATP
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: In chemiosmosis, protons flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase (Complex V); this flow drives the enzyme to make ATP from ADP + Pi — like water through a turbine.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: What is oxygen's role in oxidative phosphorylation, and what happens in its absence?
options: It is a substrate of ATP synthase; without it, protons cannot flow
It donates electrons to Complex I; without it, glycolysis stops
It directly phosphorylates ADP; without it, no NADH is made
It has no essential role in oxidative phosphorylation
It is the final electron acceptor at Complex IV
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: It is the final electron acceptor at Complex IV
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Oxygen's only metabolic job is to be the final electron acceptor at Complex IV (electrons + H⁺ + O₂ → water). Without O₂, the chain backs up and stops → no proton gradient → no ATP; NADH/FADH₂ can't be reoxidised → NAD⁺/FAD run out → Krebs cycle and link reaction halt.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: When oxidative phosphorylation halts due to lack of oxygen, what is the cell left to rely on, and what is the consequence?
options: The Krebs cycle alone, producing 30+ ATP
Anaerobic glycolysis → lactate (2 ATP) → lactic acidosis
β-oxidation of fatty acids, producing glucose
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Anaerobic glycolysis → lactate (2 ATP) → lactic acidosis
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Without O₂, the cell is left with only anaerobic glycolysis → lactate (2 ATP) → lactic acidosis. This is the biochemical basis of why hypoxia/ischaemia causes lactic acidosis and rapid energy failure.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A patient rescued from a house fire is confused and profoundly acidotic. Arterial and venous blood gases show an unusually high venous oxygen content, with a raised lactate. Which mechanism best explains this picture?
options: Carbon monoxide binding haemoglobin, reducing oxygen carriage
An uncoupler dissipating the proton gradient as heat
Cyanide blocking Complex IV, causing histotoxic hypoxia
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Cyanide blocking Complex IV, causing histotoxic hypoxia
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Cyanide blocks Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase — the O₂-accepting step) → cells can't use oxygen despite normal delivery → histotoxic hypoxia with high venous oxygen (tissues can't extract it) + lactic acidosis. It is treated with hydroxocobalamin. CO is co-inhaled in fires, but its dominant effect is on oxygen carriage, which lowers rather than raises venous oxygen content; a markedly raised lactate with a high venous oxygen saturation points to cyanide.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A newborn generates heat without shivering. Which mechanism, involving oxidative phosphorylation, is responsible?
options: Blockade of Complexes I/III by antimycin
Depletion of the hepatic glycogen stores
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Brown fat thermogenin (UCP1) uncoupling
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Brown fat thermogenin/UCP1 deliberately uncouples oxidative phosphorylation — making the membrane leaky to protons so the gradient dissipates as heat instead of ATP — producing non-shivering thermogenesis in neonates.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A patient ingests 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP) as a weight-loss agent and develops life-threatening hyperthermia. What is the mechanism?
options: It blocks Complex IV, preventing oxygen use
It inhibits ATP synthase, stopping all ATP production
It binds haemoglobin, reducing oxygen carriage
It uncouples the gradient, dissipating it as heat
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: It uncouples the gradient, dissipating it as heat
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: DNP is an uncoupler: it makes the inner membrane leaky to protons, so the proton gradient dissipates as heat instead of driving ATP synthesis, causing dangerous (potentially fatal) hyperthermia.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A child presents with recurrent energy failure affecting the brain, muscle and heart, traced to an inherited defect in the electron transport chain. Why are these particular tissues affected?
options: They are the only tissues that contain mitochondria
They depend heavily on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP
They rely exclusively on anaerobic glycolysis
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: They depend heavily on oxidative phosphorylation for ATP
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Inherited ETC defects (mitochondrial diseases) cause energy failure in high-demand tissues — brain, muscle and heart — because these tissues depend heavily on oxidative phosphorylation for their ATP.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Which statement correctly contrasts liver and muscle glycogen?
options: Both can release glucose into the blood
Only muscle glycogen can release glucose into the blood
Neither can release glucose into the blood
Muscle glycogen maintains blood glucose for the whole body
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Only liver glycogen has glucose-6-phosphatase
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Liver glycogen maintains blood glucose for the whole body and can release glucose into the blood (it has glucose-6-phosphatase). Muscle glycogen is local fuel for muscle contraction only and cannot release glucose into blood (it lacks glucose-6-phosphatase). This is why liver glycogen is the blood-glucose buffer.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Which hormone stimulates glycogenesis (glycogen storage), and in what state?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Insulin, in the fed state
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Glycogenesis (glucose → glycogen) occurs when glucose is plentiful and is stimulated by insulin in the fed state. Glycogenolysis (breakdown) is stimulated by glucagon + adrenaline in fasting/stress.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A healthy person has been fasting for roughly 18 hours. Which pathway is now the main source of blood glucose?
options: Gluconeogenesis, as glycogen stores are largely depleted
Muscle glycogenolysis releasing glucose into blood
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Gluconeogenesis, as glycogen stores are largely depleted
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: By around 18 hours hepatic glycogen is substantially depleted and gluconeogenesis supplies most of the liver's glucose output. Ketogenesis dominates only in prolonged starvation.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Where does gluconeogenesis mainly occur, and when?
options: Mainly the brain, in the fed state
Mainly red blood cells, at all times
Mainly the liver, immediately after a carbohydrate meal
Mainly the liver, during prolonged fasting
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Mainly the liver, during prolonged fasting
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Gluconeogenesis is the synthesis of new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors, occurring mainly in the liver (and some kidney), during prolonged fasting/starvation after glycogen is depleted — to keep supplying the brain and red cells (obligate glucose users).

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Which of the following is NOT a substrate for gluconeogenesis?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Fatty acids
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: The gluconeogenic precursors are lactate (Cori cycle), amino acids (especially alanine), glycerol and pyruvate. Fatty acids are not among them.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: In starvation, why can't the body make glucose directly from fat, and what does it do instead?
options: Fat has no carbon; the body uses only protein
Fatty acids are converted directly to glucose in the liver
Glycerol cannot enter gluconeogenesis, so fat is useless
Acetyl-CoA cannot be converted back to pyruvate
Fat is stored as glycogen instead
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Acetyl-CoA cannot be converted back to pyruvate
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Fatty acids cannot be converted to glucose because acetyl-CoA can't go back to pyruvate. So in starvation the body can't make glucose from fat directly — instead it makes ketones from fat (ketogenesis) to spare glucose.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: During intense exercise, lactate produced by muscle is carried to the liver and converted back to glucose, which returns to the muscle. What is this loop called, and what is its purpose?
options: The Cori cycle; it recycles lactate via the liver
The Krebs cycle; to generate NADH
The urea cycle; to remove nitrogen
The Cori cycle; to convert fat into glucose
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: The Cori cycle; it recycles lactate via the liver
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: In the Cori cycle, exercising muscle/RBCs perform anaerobic glycolysis → lactate → travels to the liver → gluconeogenesis converts lactate → glucose → returns to muscle. It recycles lactate (preventing lactic acidosis) and shifts the metabolic burden to the liver, letting muscle keep producing ATP anaerobically.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Which set of hormonal actions correctly describes the fasted (high-glucagon) state?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Glycogenolysis (release) on, gluconeogenesis on
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: In the fasted (high-glucagon) state, glucagon (+ adrenaline, cortisol) switches on glycogenolysis (release) and gluconeogenesis. The logic: glucagon = 'make/release glucose'; insulin = 'store glucose'.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Besides glucagon, cortisol and adrenaline also drive gluconeogenesis. What clinical consequence does this explain?
options: Why fatty acids can be converted to glucose
Why muscle glycogen raises blood glucose
Why the brain cannot use ketones
Why stress and steroids raise blood glucose
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Why stress and steroids raise blood glucose
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Cortisol + adrenaline are counter-regulatory hormones that drive gluconeogenesis, which is why stress/steroids raise glucose (steroid/stress hyperglycaemia).

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: As fasting progresses into prolonged starvation, which fuel becomes the main energy source, and what does it spare?
options: Ketones; sparing glucose and muscle protein
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Ketones; sparing glucose and muscle protein
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: In prolonged starvation, ketogenesis (fat → ketones) becomes the main fuel, sparing glucose and protein — the brain adapts to use ketones. The timeline is glycogenolysis (hours) → gluconeogenesis (~12–24h) → ketones (prolonged).

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A patient with type 2 diabetes is started on metformin. What is its main mechanism, and what rare adverse effect must be considered?
options: It stimulates insulin release; rare hypoglycaemia
It uncouples oxidative phosphorylation; rare hyperthermia
It inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis; rare lactic acidosis
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: It inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis; rare lactic acidosis
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Metformin inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis, lowering blood glucose (first-line in type 2 diabetes). A rare adverse effect is lactic acidosis (raised lactate).

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Why does uncontrolled diabetes lead to hyperglycaemia in terms of these glucose-raising pathways?
options: Excess insulin drives glucose into cells
Loss of glucose-6-phosphatase in the liver
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Unrestrained gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: In diabetes there is unrestrained gluconeogenesis + glycogenolysis because there is no insulin to switch these glucose-raising pathways off, producing hyperglycaemia.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: An infant presents with severe fasting hypoglycaemia and marked hepatomegaly, diagnosed as von Gierke's disease. Which enzyme deficiency is responsible?
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Von Gierke's disease is a glycogen storage disease caused by glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, leading to severe fasting hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly (the liver cannot release glucose from glycogen or gluconeogenesis).

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A patient with severe liver failure develops hypoglycaemia. Which mechanism best explains this?
options: Muscle glycogen can no longer release glucose
Excess glucagon drives glucose into cells
Reduced gluconeogenesis and glycogen, causing hypoglycaemia
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Reduced gluconeogenesis and glycogen, causing hypoglycaemia
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: The liver is the glucose factory; in liver failure, reduced gluconeogenesis and glycogen handling lead to hypoglycaemia.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: How is β-oxidation of fatty acids regulated by the fed/fasted hormones?
options: Stimulated by insulin (fed); inhibited by glucagon (fasted)
Inhibited by insulin (fed); stimulated by glucagon (fasted)
Stimulated by both insulin and glucagon
Inhibited by both insulin and glucagon
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Inhibited by insulin (fed); stimulated by glucagon (fasted)
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: β-oxidation is inhibited by insulin (fed) and stimulated by glucagon (fasted), so fat is burned only when glucose is scarce.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Which products does β-oxidation generate, and what does it require to bring fatty acids into the mitochondria?
options: Acetyl-CoA + NADH + FADH₂; requires the carnitine shuttle
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Acetyl-CoA + NADH + FADH₂; requires the carnitine shuttle
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: β-oxidation converts fatty acids → acetyl-CoA + NADH + FADH₂ in the mitochondria. Fatty acids need the carnitine shuttle to enter the mitochondria; the products feed the Krebs cycle to yield abundant ATP. β-oxidation is inhibited by insulin.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: What is the biochemical mechanism by which the liver produces ketone bodies during prolonged fasting?
options: Acetyl-CoA floods the liver faster than the Krebs cycle can use it
Glucose floods the liver and is converted to ketones
Lactate accumulates and is converted directly to ketones
Amino acids are deaminated and released as ketones
Insulin stimulates the liver to make ketones
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Acetyl-CoA floods the liver faster than the Krebs cycle can use it
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Rapid β-oxidation floods the liver with acetyl-CoA, but the Krebs cycle can't keep up because oxaloacetate is depleted (diverted to gluconeogenesis). The excess acetyl-CoA is converted by the liver into ketone bodies.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Which three substances are the ketone bodies, and which is responsible for the characteristic fruity breath?
options: Lactate, pyruvate, and citrate; lactate causes fruity breath
Acetyl-CoA, NADH, and FADH₂; NADH causes fruity breath
Acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone; acetone causes fruity breath
Glucose, glycerol, and alanine; glycerol causes fruity breath
Acetoacetate, glycerol, and acetone; acetoacetate causes fruity breath
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate, and acetone; acetone causes fruity breath
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: The ketone bodies are acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate (the two main ketones) plus acetone (the volatile one), which produces the fruity breath.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Why are ketones an especially important fuel for the brain during starvation?
options: The brain preferentially burns fatty acids, and ketones enhance this
Ketones are converted to glucose in the brain
Ketones replace oxygen as the final electron acceptor
The brain stores ketones as glycogen
The brain cannot burn fatty acids, but it can use ketones
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: The brain cannot burn fatty acids, but it can use ketones
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Ketones are a water-soluble, exportable fuel that the brain can use (the brain can't burn fatty acids directly, but it can use ketones). In starvation they become the brain's main fuel, sparing glucose and protein (less need for gluconeogenesis from muscle breakdown).

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: Why does the liver produce ketones but not use them itself?
options: The liver lacks the enzyme to use ketones, so it exports them
The liver converts all its ketones back to glucose
Ketones cannot cross the liver cell membrane
The liver only makes ketones in the fed state
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: The liver lacks the enzyme to use ketones, so it exports them
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: The liver makes ketones but can't use them (it lacks the enzyme), so it exports them to other tissues — brain, muscle and heart.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A patient on a strict low-carbohydrate diet has mildly raised ketones with a compensated, near-normal pH. How does this physiological ketosis differ from diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)?
options: Physiological ketosis is uncontrolled with severe acidosis; DKA is mild
Both produce identical, massive ketone levels
Physiological ketosis occurs only in type 1 diabetes
Physiological ketosis is controlled and compensated; DKA is not
DKA has controlled ketones because insulin is still present
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Physiological ketosis is controlled and compensated; DKA is not
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: Physiological ketosis (fasting, starvation, low-carb diet) has mild–moderate, controlled ketone levels with compensated (mild) acid-base — a regulated response to low glucose. DKA (type 1 diabetes, absolute insulin deficiency) has massive, uncontrolled ketones and a metabolic acidosis.

conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.question: A patient with type 1 diabetes presents with hyperglycaemia, dehydration, deep laboured breathing, and a fruity odour to the breath. Which sequence best explains the underlying DKA mechanism?
options: Absolute insulin deficiency → lipolysis → massive ketogenesis
Excess insulin → glucose uptake → hypoglycaemia → ketosis
Insulin resistance → impaired storage → mild ketosis
Cortisol excess → gluconeogenesis only → no acidosis
Carnitine deficiency → fat can't enter mitochondria → hypoglycaemia
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.answer: Absolute insulin deficiency → lipolysis → massive ketogenesis
conditions__LIVER__Foundations of Metabo.explanation: In type 1 diabetes, absolute insulin deficiency causes (1) hyperglycaemia (no glucose uptake) and (2) unrestrained lipolysis → massive β-oxidation → massive ketogenesis → ketones (acids) accumulate → high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis + osmotic diuresis/dehydration. Features include Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath (acetone), and dehydration.
